It's real, but it has limits. If you have a record of past bookings and which ones were no-shows, a model can usually tell higher-risk bookings from lower-risk ones. That's often useful. It gives you a likelihood for each booking, not a certainty about any one person. How much it helps depends on what you can do with the warning, such as sending reminders, overbooking a little, or calling the risky bookings. To tell you whether it's worth it for you, I need to know your situation. What kind of no-shows are you dealing with, and what would you do differently if you knew in advance which ones were likely?

Do you keep a history of past appointments, in a booking system or a spreadsheet, that shows which ones were missed? If so, what do you know about each booking (for example the date, the dentist, whether the patient is new, or how far ahead it was booked)?

transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report PR-AUC as your headline number, and give the 3% base rate next to it. **Why PR-AUC**
- With so few positives, ROC-AUC can look good even when the model is mediocre. Its false-positive rate divides by the huge pool of non-churners, so a lot of false alarms barely move it. A model can have a high ROC-AUC and still be wrong most of the time when you act on its top predictions. - PR-AUC tracks what your manager cares about. When the model flags customers as likely to churn, how many of them actually do (precision)? How many of the real churners does it catch (recall)? - A model with no skill scores a PR-AUC equal to the base rate, which is your 3%. So any PR-AUC well above 3% is a clear, easy-to-explain improvement. ROC-AUC's no-skill line sits at the midpoint of its scale, which hides how much room there is. **Caveats**
- PR-AUC depends on the churn rate, so don't compare it across segments or periods with different rates. ROC-AUC doesn't have that problem, so it is still fine as a secondary number for ranking quality. - A single AUC is abstract for a manager. If the team will contact a fixed number of customers, add precision and recall at that cutoff. It's the same story in terms they can act on. A line for the slide: "PR-AUC is X against a 3% baseline. If we contact the top N customers, about Y% of them would actually churn, and we'd reach Z% of all churners."

That's the whole answer, with no data work. If you later want those numbers computed on your own table, share it and I can set that up.
Got it, that's enough. I'm going with PR-AUC headline plus the 3% baseline, with the top-N precision/recall line for my manager. Nothing else needed.
Sounds good: PR-AUC with the 3% baseline, plus the top-N precision/recall line, should give your manager a clear picture. If you want those numbers computed on your own table later, just share it.

If the extract over-represents churners, precision on it will look better than it would on your live base. Lift against the base rate would still hold up, and we could reweight to your 4%. I'm not sure which it is. I didn't build the extract myself. Someone on the data side exported it and I haven't asked how they sampled. My guess is it was enriched with churners, since 4% of 1,200 would be about 48, not 209. 1) Fixed budgets: report precision and lift at top 10%, 20% and 30% of the holdout, each against a random pick of the same size, with bootstrap intervals. Here are your three points again, without the rough numbers I had no basis for. I need one plain yes from you before I start the build. **1) Budgets.** The report will show precision and lift at the top 10%, 20% and 30% of the holdout, and at the 200-row cutoff, labelled as such. Every figure is set against a random pick of the same size, with bootstrap intervals. Raw precision sits next to precision reweighted to your 4%. The holdout churner count prints first, before any model is fitted. That count sets how much weight any number can carry. **2) Decision rule.** I'd fix the shape now and the numbers once we have the real churner count. The count comes before any model result, so you still set the numbers before you see the holdout read. - **Baseline choice:** the better of logistic regression and gradient boosting is chosen by time-based CV inside the 80%, never on the holdout. Picking the best of two on the holdout would inflate it. - **Margin:** state it as extra churners caught within the 20% budget, not as an abstract lift figure. That is what your team would feel. - **Interval:** the lower end of the interval on the difference between the two models must be above zero, and the point estimate must also clear your margin. - **Interval width:** name a width in advance. I'll accept your proposal and we'll lock both before the holdout read.
